title: Cells, Transport and the Immune System
seo_title: Year 12 A Level Biology: Cells and the Immune System Worksheets
standard_text: Eukaryotic and prokaryotic cell structure, viruses, microscopy and magnification, cell fractionation, mitosis and the cell cycle, transport across membranes and water potential, and the immune system, vaccines and antibodies.
meta_desc: Free Year 12 A level biology worksheets on cells: organelles, magnification, mitotic index, diffusion, osmosis, active transport, antibodies, vaccines and HIV. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: 1 mm = 1000 µm; change units before dividing.
body_html:
How to think about it

Magnification = image size ÷ actual size, with both in the same unit (1 mm = 1,000 µm = 1,000,000 nm). Electron microscopes have a much higher resolution than light microscopes. The mitotic index is the percentage of cells in mitosis.

Water moves by osmosis from a higher (less negative) to a lower (more negative) water potential. In the immune response, B cells become plasma cells that make antibodies, and memory cells give a faster secondary response.

Example

Image 40 mm, magnification ×2,000. Actual size?

40 ÷ 2,000 = 0.02 mm

× 1,000

Answer: 20 µm

Example

Cell X −300 kPa, solution −500 kPa. Water moves?

from higher to lower ψ

Answer: out of cell X

Common mistakes

  • Dividing mm by magnification and calling it µm.
  • Thinking water moves to the less negative water potential.
  • Confusing antibodies with antigens.

faq.q: What is the difference between magnification and resolution?
faq.a: Magnification is how much bigger the image is; resolution is how well two close points can be seen as separate.

faq.q: Why does a vaccine protect you?
faq.a: It contains antigens that cause memory cells to be made, so a later infection triggers a fast, strong secondary response.

items.q: In a photograph a nucleus is 12.0 mm long. The magnification is ×1,500. Calculate its actual length in µm.
items.e: Actual size = image ÷ magnification = 12.0 mm ÷ 1,500 = 0.00800 mm = 8.00 µm.

items.q: In a photograph a chloroplast is 8.00 mm long. The magnification is ×2,000. Calculate its actual length in µm.
items.e: Actual size = image ÷ magnification = 8.00 mm ÷ 2,000 = 0.00400 mm = 4.00 µm.

items.q: A nucleus is 8.00 µm long. How long will its image be, in mm, at a magnification of ×2,000?
items.e: Image = actual × magnification = 16,000 µm = 16.0 mm.

items.q: What happens to a red blood cell in pure water?
c: water enters by osmosis and it bursts
items.e: Animal cells have no cell wall.

items.q: How does sodium–glucose co-transport absorb glucose in the ileum?
c: glucose is pumped out by ATP
Na⁺ diffuses into the cell down its gradient, carrying glucose with it
items.e: The gradient is set up by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump.

items.q: A scale bar 10 mm long represents 2 µm. Calculate the magnification of the drawing.
What are the ribosomes of prokaryotes?
items.e: Mitochondria and chloroplasts also have 70S ribosomes.

items.q: What is facilitated diffusion?
c: passive movement of molecules through channel or carrier proteins
items.e: Down a concentration gradient.

items.q: What is active transport?
c: movement against a concentration gradient using ATP and carrier proteins
items.e: Carrier proteins change shape.

items.e: The heaviest organelles settle at the lowest speed.

items.q: What does a scanning electron microscope produce?

items.e: Its resolution is lower than a TEM.

items.q: Which microscope has the highest resolution?
items.e: Electrons have a much shorter wavelength than light.

items.q: What does cholesterol do in a cell membrane?
c: it reduces fluidity and makes the membrane more stable
items.e: It sits between the phospholipids.

items.q: Why can oxygen diffuse straight through the phospholipid bilayer?
items.e: Ions need channel proteins.

items.q: Why is a virus not considered a living cell?
c: it has no cytoplasm or ribosomes and can only replicate inside a host cell
items.e: Viruses are acellular.

items.q: What happens in anaphase of mitosis?
c: sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles
items.e: The centromeres divide.

items.q: Which organelle is the site of aerobic respiration?
items.e: Mitochondria make most of the cell's ATP.

items.q: What is the function of the Golgi apparatus?
c: modifying and packaging proteins and lipids into vesicles
items.e: It also makes lysosomes.

items.q: Cell X has a water potential of −1200 kPa and cell Y has −400 kPa. Which has the higher water potential?
items.e: The value closer to zero (−400 kPa) is higher.

items.q: Why is cancer linked to uncontrolled mitosis?
c: mutations in genes that control the cell cycle
items.e: Tumours form from rapidly dividing cells.

items.q: What do lysosomes contain?
items.e: They digest worn-out organelles and pathogens.

items.q: What is a monoclonal antibody?
c: an antibody made from a single clone of B cells
items.e: Used in pregnancy tests and targeted drugs.

items.q: What is the humoral response?
c: the response involving B cells and antibodies
the response of T cells only
items.e: Antibodies are in body fluids.

items.q: What is antigenic variability?
c: a pathogen's antigens change, so memory cells do not recognise them
items.e: This is why flu vaccines change each year.

items.q: Why might a transplanted organ be rejected?
c: the body recognises its antigens as foreign
the organ has no blood supply
items.e: Immunosuppressant drugs reduce the risk.

items.q: What do cytotoxic T cells do?
c: kill infected body cells by making holes in them (perforin)
items.e: Part of the cellular response.

items.q: What is an ethical issue with vaccines?
c: testing may involve animals or there may be side effects
items.e: There are also questions about compulsory vaccination.

items.q: Why do antibiotics not work against HIV?
c: viruses have no cell wall or ribosomes for antibiotics to target
items.e: Antiretroviral drugs are used instead.

items.q: How does a vaccine give protection?
c: it contains antigens that cause memory cells to be made
items.e: A later infection gives a fast secondary response.

items.q: What is agglutination?
items.e: Each antibody has two binding sites.

items.q: Which white blood cells mature in the thymus?
items.e: B cells mature in the bone marrow.

items.q: What is clonal selection?
c: the B or T cell with the matching receptor is selected and divides
items.e: Then clonal expansion happens.

items.q: How does an antibody's structure suit its job?
c: it has two variable regions that bind specific antigens and a constant region
items.e: Four polypeptide chains joined by disulfide bridges.

items.q: What is the cellular response?
items.e: T cells respond to antigens on cells.

items.q: What is active immunity?
c: your own immune system makes antibodies after exposure to an antigen
items.e: It gives long-lasting memory.

items.q: What is an antibody?
c: a protein that binds to a specific antigen
items.e: Made by plasma cells.

items.q: What is an antigen?
c: a molecule that triggers an immune response
a protein made by B cells
a type of white blood cell
items.e: Usually a protein on the surface of a cell or virus.

items.q: How does the ELISA test detect an antigen?
c: an enzyme-linked antibody gives a colour change
items.e: Washing removes unbound antibodies.

items.q: Which cells make antibodies?
items.e: Plasma cells are made from B cells.

items.q: How does HIV cause AIDS?
c: it destroys T helper cells, weakening the immune system
items.e: Opportunistic infections follow.

items.q: What is herd immunity?
c: when enough people are vaccinated that a disease cannot spread easily
items.e: It protects unvaccinated people too.
